findings.description: The R2 wrapper now strips by VALUE, which fixed the backtick case, but `wrapper_is_live` still measures liveness against the probe's OWN synthetic anchor while the suite measures coverage against the CORPUS anchor — and those two strings behave differently under `!r`. `ANCHOR_TEXT = "if len(val) >= 2 and val[0] == val[-1]:"` contains no quote characters, so `repr()` leaves it intact and `out.replace(anchor, "")` removes it. The #117 corpus anchor an archive-drawn case must use is `if len(val) >= 2 and val[0] == val[-1] and val[0] in "\"'"` (archive/2026-08-10-issue-117/tasks/T-001.md:57), which carries both quote characters, so `repr()` escapes them and the raw anchor is no longer a substring of the message — the strip silently removes nothing. Built and ran it: refA with `f"was {anchor!r}"` instead of backticks reports `ok  R2 diagnostic: the wrapper actually strips the anchor at runtime` and then `FAIL R2 diagnostic: removing the quoted anchor turns the suite red / rc=0 — no case asserts the anchor is quoted`, against a suite whose M9 case asserts exactly that and passes. This is r5's blocker in a new location, and it is worse than r5's: r5's version failed loudly, this one first tells the checker its precondition held. The rubric's one named escape hatch is R10 caller placement, which does not cover it, and `wrapper_is_live` printing ok actively rules out the 'seam does not match this factoring' reading the rubric otherwise offers. The preamble's r6 note claims the repair was 'Verified across backticks, `!r`, and no quoting at all' — true only for the probe's escape-free fixture. Fix: assert liveness on the same message the suite reads, or compare a normalized form (strip both `repr(anchor)` and `anchor`), and have the rubric tell the checker that a mutation which no-ops is a probe limitation to re-check by hand rather than a missing case.
findings.evidence: /tmp/con-r6-7dQGzD/atk-reprquote — probe.py suite-coverage; repr-escape demonstrated directly: `anchor in f'{anchor!r}'` is False for the corpus anchor and True for probe.py:512 ANCHOR_TEXT

findings.description: The r7 fold dropped the R2 seam requirement from C-9's TEXT and left it standing as an assertion in the check, with a failure detail that states a requirement the clause no longer makes. r4 put it in C-9's text explicitly ('requires the R2 diagnostic to be built by a function named `r2_anchor_message`'); the current text says only that each change 'has a case in `test_check_job_spec.py` that goes red when that change is reverted'. Nothing in the constitution, and nothing in spec.md — whose 'Start here' names `:588-615` as 'the R2 branch that builds the diagnostic' — requires a named function. I built the ordinary reading: the message composed inline in `check_citation_rules`, no helper. It passes C-5 (probe exits 0, [A] and [B] both name the anchor and its position), passes C-6 with 235 green including an M9 case asserting the anchor is quoted, and hits `FAIL R2 diagnostic: `r2_anchor_message` exists as the seam / no named function builds the R2 diagnostic; C-9 requires one`. The whole R2 block is then SKIPPED, so the checker gets no evidence about R2 coverage at all and no instruction for what to do with its absence. Fix: put the seam back in C-9's text as a requirement on the implementation (r4's argument for it still holds — without a named seam there is no way to remove the anchor without also killing R2's pre-job cases), or, if the fold meant to drop it, tell the checker in the rubric how to rule when the seam is absent.
findings.evidence: /tmp/con-r6-7dQGzD/atk-inline — r2-anchor exit 0, test_check_job_spec.py 235 passed 0 failed, suite-coverage FAILED (1) on the seam assertion

findings.description: The probe's `revert_adjacency` failure detail tells the reader the opposite of what C-9's rubric rules. The rubric says 'a relaxation living in `find_r10_violation` rather than the predicate is a legitimate implementation the revert cannot reach, and there the question is whether some case still fails when you undo the relaxation by hand.' The detail the checker actually reads says 'C-9 requires it inside that predicate ... Move the modifier walk into `_governs_plural_noun` rather than its caller.' I built the caller variant (refB): every script clause green, and suite-coverage prints that detail. Following the rubric I undid the relaxation by hand at the call site and the suite went red on three M7 assertions, so refB is genuinely covered and rules PASS. A checker who weights the specific machine output over the general prose fails correct work — the r5 blocker's shape surviving into the very text written to retire it. Fix: rewrite probe.py:773-777's detail to say what the rubric says ('the adjacency decision is not being made in this predicate; if it lives in `find_r10_violation`, undo it there by hand and re-run the suite') and drop the 'C-9 requires' sentence.

findings.description: The rubric's three git reads all go blind on a STAGED working tree, which is the ordinary shape when a worker has run `git add` before reporting. Verified in refA: with `test_check_job_spec.py` staged, `git diff -- .agent-guild/scripts/test_check_job_spec.py` returns 0 lines, `git diff $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD -- <path>` returns 0 lines, and `git status --porcelain` returns `M  .agent-guild/scripts/test_check_job_spec.py` — non-empty, so the clause's FAIL-on-empty branch does not fire, but carrying no case content for the checker to rule 'where each case's input comes from' against. The archive-drawn half is then unjudgeable and the checker has to improvise or return blocked. r6's repair fixed the committed-tree hole and left the staged one. Fix: make the first read `git diff HEAD -- .agent-guild/scripts/test_check_job_spec.py`, which covers staged and unstaged together — verified at 119 lines on the same staged tree where the current first read returns 0.

The new revision-note guard is inaccurate in the one direction that costs something. It reads 'Nothing below is a statement about the current text. The clauses themselves are the only current statement, and a decompose step should excerpt those rather than this history' (constitution.md:48-50). `SPEC DIVERGENCE` sits BELOW it, at :279-285, and is not history: it is a live ruling by the user that C-5 overrides spec.md's 'distinct from the two line numbers it already reports', ending in a direct instruction to Phase 1 — 'Anything excerpting the spec into a worker's brief must carry C-5's text instead, not the criterion's.' The guard as written licenses a decompose step to skip exactly the paragraph that keeps the wrong spec sentence out of a worker's brief, and I confirmed the divergence is real: the spec sentence is false for case B, where the anchor sits on the citing line and there is no third distinct number to report. Fix: scope the guard to the REVISION notes by name, or move SPEC DIVERGENCE above it.
findings.evidence: .agent-guild/state/constitution.md:44-50 against :279-285; case B confirmed by probe.py r2-anchor [B] on every variant built this round

findings.description: C-9's stated reason for existing rests on a false fact about this repo. The text says 'This is the job's only lasting regression net: `.agent-guild/state/` is gitignored in full, so the probe harness every other clause runs is deleted at teardown and the suite is what remains.' `.gitignore:5-6` reads `.agent-guild/state/*` followed by `!.agent-guild/state/archive/`, and `git ls-files .agent-guild/state/archive/` counts 378 tracked files. State is not gitignored in full; the archive is deliberately tracked. The conclusion survives — `git check-ignore -v .agent-guild/state/checks/probe.py` confirms the harness itself is ignored — but a checker re-deriving the sentence finds it false, and the exception matters to this very clause, since the archive-drawn cases it requires only keep working BECAUSE the archive travels with the repo. Fix: 'everything under `.agent-guild/state/` except `archive/` is gitignored, so the probe harness ... is deleted at teardown while the corpus these cases draw from travels with the repo.'

The fold kept C-10's archive-drawn requirement and its rulings but not its failing example. C-9's failing example describes only the discrimination half — 'all three fixes land, every script-checked clause passes, and `test_check_job_spec.py` is untouched'. A suite carrying three genuinely discriminating cases built from invented fixtures violates C-9's text and matches no failing example the clause offers, which is the falsifiability property this document holds its own clauses to. Fix: add one sentence — 'or the three cases exist and discriminate, but their paperwork was invented for the test rather than drawn from the archive, so nothing shows the rules would have caught the real thing.'
